claims.text: Retention of a uniform, single-phase disordered structure in high-entropy nanoalloys is governed primarily by kinetic limitations rather than exclusively by configurational entropy.
Restricted atomic diffusion caused by a high density of grain boundaries and related interfaces is the relevant kinetic limitation.
The proposed initial material is an equiatomic, chemically uniform, disordered high-entropy nanoalloy.
The nanoalloy microstructure can be tuned to provide controlled grain sizes and grain-boundary densities.
Standardized processing minimizes initial chemical segregation.
Fine-grained specimens have a higher grain-boundary density than coarse-grained specimens.
Exposure at about 850 °C for the selected duration permits significant atomic diffusion while an inert atmosphere suppresses severe oxidation.
Grain boundaries and interfaces act as kinetic barriers to atomic diffusion.
Increasing grain-boundary and interface density impedes atomic diffusion at elevated temperature.
Restricted diffusion slows thermodynamically driven phase separation and chemical ordering.
Slower phase separation and ordering stabilize the disordered solid solution when configurational entropy alone is insufficient.
After high-temperature exposure, fine-grained samples will exhibit less phase segregation and greater chemical uniformity than coarse-grained samples.
Coarse-grained samples will show an earlier onset or greater extent of nanoscale phase separation or elemental segregation.
The prediction applies above 800 °C under inert or non-oxidizing conditions.
Oxidation or other environmental reactions can dominate and invalidate the predicted grain-size effect.
Non-equilibrium processing can independently alter microstructural evolution and thereby place the system outside the prediction's scope.
The magnitude of the grain-size effect may depend on the specific alloy system and minor compositional variations.

Statistically indistinguishable phase segregation and chemical inhomogeneity in fine- and coarse-grained samples would falsify the claim that enhanced grain-boundary density is the primary stabilizing factor.
